title: Ron And Tammys

jokes.text: Budgetary Thunderdome.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining the upcoming budget meeting where all departments argue for more money.
jokes.punchline: She names it 'Budgetary Thunderdome' — a grandiose pop-culture nickname for a mundane government meeting.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie Knope move: treating a mundane bureaucratic event with outsized cinematic drama. The economy is excellent — two words do all the work. Character-specific because Leslie's enthusiasm for government process is her defining trait. Not quite at the top tier because the pop-culture reference (Mad Max) does most of the lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so tomorrow's budget meeting is going to be intense. We need to prepare for the thunderdome of municipal finance. It's going to be brutal, it's going to be chaotic, and honestly, it's going to make Mad Max look like a PTA meeting.

jokes.text: Our secret weapon in this budgetary battle? Ron. Every time another department asks for more money, he just stares them down until they back off and, or, wet themselves.
jokes.setup: Leslie builds up the 'secret weapon' reveal with dramatic framing.
jokes.punchline: The weapon is just Ron staring at people, with the escalating detail that they 'wet themselves.'
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels: the misdirection of a 'secret weapon' being a person doing nothing, and the character-specific gag that Ron's silent disapproval is so powerful it causes incontinence. The 'and, or, wet themselves' pause construction is a nice bit of writing craft — Leslie correcting herself mid-sentence makes it feel natural and funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron is our secret weapon.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, when people meet Ron, they're either really into him or they back off slowly.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And then they wet themselves.

jokes.text: First of all, income tax is illegal.
jokes.setup: Ron is being told he's being audited by the IRS and needs to take it seriously.
jokes.punchline: His first response is to declare income tax illegal — completely on-brand libertarian deflection.
jokes.explanation: Four words that are perfectly Ron Swanson. It requires zero setup beyond the character existing. The economy is nearly perfect — it's the most Ron Swanson thing he could possibly say in this situation, and it lands instantly because the audience already knows the character. High character integration score because this joke simply does not exist without Ron Swanson specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Income tax is illegal. I've checked with the constitution multiple times. It's not in there.

jokes.text: Tammy is a psychological mastermind. This is just another way for her to put her hand up my keister and control me like a puppet.
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining why he doesn't trust the tax audit.
jokes.punchline: The puppet metaphor escalates into viscerally specific physical imagery — 'hand up my keister' is both absurd and telling.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'keister' and 'control me like a puppet' takes what could be a generic complaint and makes it vivid and funny. Ron delivering this with complete seriousness is the key. Slightly bloated — could be tighter — but the puppet imagery earns its length.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She has this uncanny ability to make me do things I don't want to do. It's like she's got invisible strings attached to me, pulling me in whatever direction she wants. I'm a puppet, and she's the puppet master.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Except the strings are made of disappointment and regret, and instead of a puppet stage, it's my entire life. And instead of an audience, it's just me, alone, wondering where it all went wrong.

jokes.text: Jail, Ron. Ron, jail. Jail, Ron. Jail. You could go to jail. Jail. Jail. Jail. Are you broken?
jokes.setup: Leslie desperately tries to convey the severity of a federal tax audit to an unresponsive Ron.
jokes.punchline: The repetition escalates into pure absurdity, culminating in Andy asking 'Are you broken?' — treating Ron like a malfunctioning machine.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured escalation. The repetition of 'Jail/Ron' starts as desperation and becomes comedic incantation, then the punchline 'Are you broken?' recontextualizes everything — Andy treats Ron as a frozen computer. The construction is smart: it's funny the first three times, then it becomes absurdist, then Andy's flat question caps it perfectly. High structure and economy scores because every word is doing work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, this is serious. You could go to jail. Jail, Ron. Jail. Do you understand? Jail. You're going to jail. Jail!

jokes.text: Operation Rescue Ron is starting. Don't worry. I will think of a better name for it by tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Leslie launches into action-hero mode, naming her plan dramatically.
jokes.punchline: She immediately acknowledges the name is bad and promises to fix it later — deflating her own grandiosity.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's self-awareness about her own naming conventions is a delightful character beat. The joke works because she commits so fully to the operation name while simultaneously undermining it. The immediate self-correction is the comedic move, and it's well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, you've said the word 'jail' about 47 times in the last ten minutes. I'm starting to think you might need professional help.

jokes.text: Hey, thanks for texting me to hang out. I really felt like we'd developed a cool friendship, and it... Anyway, it was just nice to have that validated.
jokes.setup: Ben receives what he thinks is a friendly hangout text from Tom.
jokes.punchline: His sincere, emotionally vulnerable reaction to a text that was purely transactional reveals his loneliness and earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Ben's social awkwardness and earnestness are perfectly captured here. The trailing '...Anyway, it was just nice to have that validated' is the key — he catches himself being too vulnerable and tries to recover, which only makes it more vulnerable. Strong character integration for Ben specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Operation Rescue Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, I know. It's a bad name.

jokes.text: No, of course. Yeah, no. I'll just put on my Star Wars pajamas and sit in my mom's basement and pore over some spreadsheets.
jokes.setup: Tom has just called Ben a nerd (twice) and suggested 'nerd stuff probably really excites you.'
jokes.punchline: Ben responds with sarcastic over-commitment to the nerd stereotype, listing specific nerdy details with deadpan resignation.
jokes.explanation: Solid sarcasm with good specificity (Star Wars pajamas, mom's basement). The joke is in Ben's resigned delivery — he's not quite denying it, just committing sarcastically to the bit. Not groundbreaking but well-executed. The 'That sounds great' response from Tom missing the sarcasm entirely would be the visual kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom! Hey! I'm so glad you're here. You know, I just wanted to say how much your friendship means to me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Aw, man, that's nice. What's this about?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Nothing, I just appreciate you. You've always been there for me, and I don't say it enough.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, what do you want?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Can I borrow twenty thousand dollars?

jokes.text: Something called 'break even analysis tables'? Oh, break evens? Those are really fun.
jokes.setup: Tom frames the financial documents as intimidating and incomprehensible.
jokes.punchline: Ben's genuine enthusiasm for break-even analyses — calling them 'really fun' — reveals his nerd nature more effectively than any insult could.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly efficient character joke. Ben's unironic delight at 'break even analysis tables' — the face-to-face answer to Tom's insult — is funnier than any sarcastic comeback. The specificity of 'break evens' as a term of endearment is key. Strong character integration because this joke ONLY works with Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're right, Tom. I am a nerd. In fact, I'm going to lean into it. I'm going to start wearing a pocket protector, get really into D&D, and I'm going to write a 47-page technical manual on the proper way to organize a filing system.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And you know what? I'm going to enjoy every second of it, because at least nerds have hobbies that don't involve getting kicked out of Applebee's.

jokes.text: It's almost too easy. [beat] I can hear you. I know you can, Ben. That's how easy it is.
jokes.setup: Tom mutters to himself (or to the camera) about how easy it is to manipulate Ben.
jokes.punchline: Ben hears him. Tom doesn't even bother to cover — doubling down 'That's how easy it is' turns the exposure into another flex.
jokes.explanation: Tight, smart construction. The joke has two beats: Tom's aside, then Ben's interruption, then Tom's confident non-apology escalation. The structure is the joke — Tom's shamelessness being revealed AND confirmed in the same exchange. 'That's how easy it is' repurposes his own exposure as proof of his thesis. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Ben, I need your help moving to California tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, of course! I'd be happy to help you move.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Great! I'm leaving in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, tomorrow? Like... you're moving away? For good?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got that job offer and I'm taking it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh. So when you said you needed my help... you meant right now. You're actually leaving. We're not gonna... I thought we were best friends.

jokes.text: I've heavily invested in gold, which I've buried in several different locations around Pawnee. Or have I?
jokes.setup: Leslie notes there are no bank statements, implying Ron's finances are a mess.
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals he's buried gold around town, then immediately introduces paranoid doubt — 'Or have I?' — suggesting even more elaborate deception.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's strongest purely character-based joke. 'Or have I?' is doing enormous work — it reveals that Ron's gold-hoarding is so serious he maintains plausible deniability even while confessing to it, suggesting multiple layers of misdirection. It's funny, it's surprising, it perfectly expresses his libertarian paranoia, and it PAYS OFF LATER when the decoy gold reveal happens. High rewatch bonus. The economy is impeccable — three words completely detonate the previous sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, I'm going to manipulate you right now, but I'm going to be totally honest about it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? Tom, no—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: See, I'm already doing it. You're so confused right now that you can't even mount a proper defense. This is classic misdirection through transparency.

jokes.text: That is a gentleman's agreement. I made that man a dining room table in exchange for 60 feet of copper pipe and a half pig.
jokes.setup: April finds what appears to be a suspicious document and asks if it's a drug deal.
jokes.punchline: Ron clarifies it's a barter arrangement — but the specifics (copper pipe + half pig) are so precise and pre-modern that they become absurd.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on specificity — '60 feet of copper pipe and a half pig' is so precise it sounds both completely believable for Ron and completely absurd for any other person. The word 'gentleman's agreement' elevating a medieval barter transaction is the comedic frame. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, these tax receipts are a nightmare. You have a receipt for 'Government Waste' dated three years ago with no other information.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's a legitimate business expense. I was protesting.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You also have a receipt that just says 'Whiskey' with a question mark.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I wasn't sure if it was whiskey. Could've been scotch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, they're the same thing!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Not to the IRS they're not. I'm very thorough.

jokes.text: Every 30 days, I buy shotgun shells and cigarettes, and send them home to my mom. That's so sweet. Your mom sounds kickass.
jokes.setup: A recurring charge of $140/month is found in Ron's records — presented as if it might be something sinister or embarrassing.
jokes.punchline: It's a monthly care package of shotgun shells and cigarettes to his mom — both the act and April's sincere approval are the joke.
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke that fires perfectly. The reveal of the care package contents (shotgun shells + cigarettes) is funny on its own — the dark-subversive vision of maternal love. But April's genuine, warm response ('Your mom sounds kickass') is the better joke — her approval is so pitch-perfect to April's character that it doubles the laugh. The juxtaposition of tenderness and danger is beautifully handled.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't keep bank statements. I don't believe in them.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Or have I?

jokes.text: My first ex-wife's name is Tammy. My second ex-wife's name is Tammy. [pause] My mom's name is Tamara. [pause] She goes by Tammy.
jokes.setup: Ron reveals the first Tammy, then the second Tammy — each pause building the pattern.
jokes.punchline: The triple-Tammy reveal: his mom is also named Tammy — delivered with three separate pauses to maximize comedic timing.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes and a Parks and Rec all-timer. The structure is textbook comedy escalation: establish a pattern (Tammy 1, Tammy 2), subvert it (Tamara — relief), then devastate it (she goes by Tammy). The three pauses are the structural genius — the writer trusted the silence to do the work. Character integration is total: only Ron Swanson could have this backstory delivered this earnestly. The joke earns every second of its length. High quotability because it requires context to appreciate fully — it rewards show knowledge.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron, what is this? Are you dealing drugs?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. I'm trading wood chips for a new engine block. The man needed mulch for his garden, I need an engine. It's called capitalism.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's literally just bartering.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I prefer to call it a free market transaction. Now if you'll excuse me, I have to go trade three cords of firewood for dental work.

jokes.text: That is Walt Morphling. He was the Director of Public Health, but he had to retire at 46 because he had diabetes. That is sad, but also, in this town, understandable.
jokes.setup: A PSA featuring an unhealthy-looking man is playing on screen.
jokes.punchline: 'That is sad, but also, in this town, understandable' — the throwaway civic cynicism undercuts her own government optimism.
jokes.explanation: The qualifier 'in this town, understandable' is the comedic gem — it's a backhanded insult to Pawnee delivered with complete civic pride. Leslie simultaneously mourns and accepts the inevitability of Pawnee's unhealthiness. The deadpan-understatement register is perfect for her character.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I send my mother a care package every month. It costs about $140.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's just weapons and tobacco.

jokes.text: Scary? Posh? Baby? Those are the Spice Girls. I just got caught up in my own thoughts.
jokes.setup: Leslie is listing wardrobe options for the PSA (casual, formal, semi-formal, sporty...) and keeps going.
jokes.punchline: She lists Spice Girl nicknames without realizing it, then catches herself and explains without embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Leslie joke because it reveals her inner monologue drifted into Spice Girls territory mid-sentence, and she owns it completely with zero shame. 'I just got caught up in my own thoughts' is a perfect non-apology. The structure (list goes wrong, recognition, explanation) is tight and well-executed. The joke only works with Leslie because her brain-to-mouth filter is so thin.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your mom sounds kickass.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She is. Her name is Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've also dated a Tammy. And another Tammy. And I'm currently in a relationship with a Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You have a type.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a pattern.

jokes.text: Uh, no, because you just approved the idea, like, three seconds ago.
jokes.setup: Chris immediately asks for a script after Leslie pitches and approves the PSA idea.
jokes.punchline: Leslie points out the chronological impossibility with amused exasperation.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke that establishes Chris's over-the-top enthusiasm, but not particularly original. The humor is straightforward situational irony.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've been married three times. All three of my wives were named Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My mother's name is Tammy. My current mistress's name is Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a sister named Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: …I see what that sounds like now.

jokes.text: NBA's on strike, so we got him for only, like, 75% of his original NBA salary.
jokes.setup: Ben sees actual NBA player Detlef Schrempf hanging around Entertainment 720.
jokes.punchline: Tom explains the NBA lockout savings as if this is smart business, not insane waste — 75% of an NBA salary is still enormous.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the gap between Tom's self-congratulation (he got a deal!) and the insanity of hiring an NBA player at any percentage of his salary to hang out. The NBA lockout reference is a nice topical touch. Character integration strong — only Tom would pitch this as fiscal responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's so ironic. The health director got the exact disease he was supposed to prevent.

jokes.text: Your name is Angelo. Angelo, thank you so much for coming out. Get a thicker tie. It looks weird on you. Makes your head look like a fish.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio meets Ben for the first time and immediately takes over his identity.
jokes.punchline: He renames Ben 'Angelo,' welcomes him warmly, then immediately insults his tie with the specific and baffling simile 'makes your head look like a fish.'
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's manic energy is perfectly deployed here. The 'fish' simile is the comedic peak — it's specific enough to sound like a real observation but bizarre enough to be meaningless. The structure (warmth → insult → non sequitur) captures Jean-Ralphio perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, I guess that's just Pawnee. The health director has diabetes, the parks department is completely dysfunctional, and somehow that's just... normal here.

jokes.text: Your new nickname is Jell-O Shot. What do you think about that, 'J-Shot'?
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio has already renamed Ben 'Angelo,' then immediately decides he hates that name.
jokes.punchline: He renames Ben 'Jell-O Shot' and immediately further abbreviates it to 'J-Shot' — the escalation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Ben's identity being erased by Jean-Ralphio continues. 'Jell-O Shot' is funny for the randomness; J-Shot is funnier because he's already creating a nickname for the nickname. The callback to 'Angelo' being rejected adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So I'm thinking about updating my wardrobe. You know, maybe I'll go with something a little more... Posh.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Or maybe Sporty. Or Scary. Or Baby.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait... why do all my fashion ideas sound like girl groups?

jokes.text: If you don't mind me asking, how much are they paying you? A hundred thousand dollars a year with full medical.
jokes.setup: Ben approaches a model who seems to be serving as a receptionist — she herself doesn't know her role.
jokes.punchline: $100,000/year with full medical benefits — for someone who 'doesn't really know' if she's a receptionist.
jokes.explanation: The structure is efficient: uncertain receptionist → enormous salary reveal. Works as a component of the running E 720 financial absurdity gag. 'I guess. I don't really know' from the receptionist is a bonus character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? Seventy-five percent of an NBA player's salary is a bargain for a failing business. That's basically free money.

jokes.text: I mean, I would guess they'll be bankrupt by the end of this sentence.
jokes.setup: Ben has just learned the uncertain receptionist makes $100K/year.
jokes.punchline: His talking-head confession — 'bankrupt by the end of this sentence' — uses the speed of the sentence itself as the unit of measurement for their burn rate.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy of language — 'bankrupt by the end of this sentence' is a genuinely clever construction that uses the medium (spoken word, specific timeline of a sentence) to express how rapidly E 720 is burning money. It's not just a hyperbole; it's a precise and self-aware hyperbole. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted and repeated. Ben's accountant brain expressing horror through financial metaphors is perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: From now on, I'm calling you... Brando.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why Brando?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Because you look like a discount Marlon Brando. A Marlon Blando, if you will. Also, those khakis are a crime against fashion. You look like a sad accountant at a Sandals resort.

jokes.text: Is this true? You only spent $40 on clothes in the past five years?
jokes.setup: April is going through Ron's financial records.
jokes.punchline: Ron's total clothing expenditure over five years is $40 — a detail that perfectly characterizes his ascetic anti-consumerism.
jokes.explanation: A good character gag that lands primarily on recognition — 'of course Ron would spend $40 on clothes in 5 years.' The laugh is more of a knowing nod than a surprise. Strong character integration but lower scores elsewhere because it's a bit predictable once you know Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Actually, wait. I'm gonna call you Travesty.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's worse.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: No it's not. It's a portmanteau of 'travesty' and 'majesty.'

jokes.text: Technically, I've known her since I was born. She was a candy striper at the hospital. She helped deliver me.
jokes.setup: April asks how Ron met Tammy One.
jokes.punchline: He's known her literally since birth — she was his delivery nurse as a candy striper, which establishes the deeply unsettling timeline of their eventual relationship.
jokes.explanation: The comedic horror builds as you process the implications. The joke is in what's NOT said — Ron delivers this as a normal biographical fact, while the audience calculates the math. The candy striper detail makes it more specific and therefore more disturbing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: How much are we paying her?

dialogue.speaker: Model/Receptionist
dialogue.line: I don't know what I'm doing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're paying her a massive salary.

jokes.text: We first took up together when I was 15. [April reacts] It was a little scandalous, but everyone feared her, so they kept their mouths shut.
jokes.setup: Ron continues the story of how Tammy One controlled an entire small town through fear.
jokes.punchline: Everyone knew it was inappropriate but were too scared to say anything — the community's silence as a punchline.
jokes.explanation: The dark comedy here is that Ron's entire backstory with Tammy One is played completely straight while being genuinely horrifying. 'Everyone feared her, so they kept their mouths shut' is a great line — the town's complicity explained with complete matter-of-factness. April's reaction beat (implied 'Awesome. Oh, my God.') is the other half of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, so if we factor in the cost of the gazebo, the permits, the insurance, the maintenance crew, the port-a-potties, and the DJ... we're looking at approximately $47,000 in overhead costs.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Which means, given our current budget, we'll be completely out of money by... next Thursday at 2 PM.

jokes.text: I don't even know her, but she's my hero.
jokes.setup: Ron has been describing Tammy One's disturbing control over him and a small town.
jokes.punchline: April, who relates to chaos and the subversion of authority, instantly idolizes this woman.
jokes.explanation: April's instant, sincere idolization of a woman who groomed Ron as a teen and threw acid on Tammy Two is completely in character and completely absurd. The joke is tight and the character integration is excellent — April admiring authority-subverting chaos agents is her core trait.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy One and I met when I was in high school. She was my history teacher.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was 17 years old.

jokes.text: She did, however, teach me everything I know. Sunday school, sex. She was my math teacher in middle school and my babysitter, and she taught drivers ed.
jokes.setup: Ron has acknowledged Tammy One is a 'hellacious nightmare.'
jokes.punchline: He lists the ways she formed him: 'Sunday school, sex' in the same breath, then the escalating roles (math teacher, babysitter, drivers ed).
jokes.explanation: The list structure is brilliant. 'Sunday school, sex' placed side by side as if equally mundane is the primary comedic shock. Then the escalating list of roles she held in Ron's life (each one adding another layer of inappropriate influence) escalates the discomfort beautifully. Delivered with Ron's complete deadpan sincerity, which makes it both funnier and darker. High structure score for the list construction.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy One taught me everything I know. She taught me how to cook, how to provide for a family, how to treat a woman with respect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And the accumulating inappropriate power dynamics.

jokes.text: I don't think it will be necessary for you to speak again while I'm here.
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces herself with her full professional title.
jokes.punchline: Tammy One immediately and completely shuts her down — dismissing Leslie's authority with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: The economy of this dismissal is remarkable — one sentence completely establishes Tammy One's dominance and Leslie's helplessness against her. It's also funny because Leslie, one of the show's most competent characters, is immediately and completely neutralized. Great character contrast comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Hi! I'm Leslie Knope, I work here in the Parks Department, and I just wanted to introduce myself and—

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Why do I only date brunettes? You know, sometimes, you eat chicken and you get food poisoning, and then even the sight of chicken makes you sick? Tammy One is my blonde chicken.
jokes.setup: Ron muses to the camera about his attraction patterns.
jokes.punchline: His entire explanation of avoiding blonde women comes down to Tammy One being his 'blonde chicken' — a deeply specific trauma metaphor.
jokes.explanation: The food poisoning analogy is unexpected and somehow both clinical and emotionally revealing. 'Tammy One is my blonde chicken' is the kind of quotable line that gets remembered. Ron's tendency to explain deeply personal trauma through practical, food-related metaphors is perfectly in character. The joke earns its setup length.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I only date brunettes because blondes are like cotton candy - pretty to look at, but ultimately empty and forgettable. Redheads are spicy, unpredictable, wild cards. But brunettes? Brunettes are like a well-prepared meal. Substantial. Dependable. Satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy, however, is like food poisoning. She seemed fine at first, but then she got inside me and made me violently ill for years.

jokes.text: Good God, Ronald. This is a much bigger mess than I imagined. You'll take a week off from work. We'll do a complete overhaul of your finances. I'll need access to all of your accounts. And your home.
jokes.setup: The 'audit' is framed as legitimate IRS activity.
jokes.punchline: Each demand escalates beyond auditing into total life takeover — 'And your home' as a casual afterthought.
jokes.explanation: The escalating demands with 'And your home' as the quiet clincher work well. The comedy is in watching Tammy One's control expand scope with each sentence, with Ron seemingly unable to stop it. Good escalation structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Is that necessary?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: Ron, I've been married to you for two years. Everything I do is necessary.

jokes.text: Is that necessary? Oh, are we playing a game where everyone says something stupid?
jokes.setup: Ron meekly asks if Tammy needing access to his home is necessary.
jokes.punchline: Tammy's withering response — 'are we playing a game where everyone says something stupid?' — treats his reasonable question as idiotic.
jokes.explanation: This is a masterfully contemptuous line. 'Are we playing a game where everyone says something stupid?' reframes his entirely reasonable objection as stupidity. The economy is excellent. It also shows why Tammy One is terrifying — she can make sense feel like nonsense.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's... Burt Macklin.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, it's Andy. I'm sorry, I panicked.

jokes.text: You. What is your name? Tim. Tim Buckanowski. Really? No. Andy Dwyer.
jokes.setup: Tammy One turns her attention to Andy with intimidating authority.
jokes.punchline: Andy gives a fake name under her intense gaze, immediately breaks and confesses his real name.
jokes.explanation: Andy's immediate capitulation under Tammy One's pressure is both character-specific (Andy folds immediately) and funny in the rhythm — 'Really? No.' — where 'Really?' implies she can see through the lie and Andy just... confesses. The name 'Tim Buckanowski' is a funny fake name choice.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: Ron will be in prison within five years. I've seen it. He'll be the wife of a man named Curtis who makes license plates in the yard. Ron will have a tattoo of a horse on his neck. He'll write me letters in a childish scrawl, begging me to send him cigarettes and skin lotion.

jokes.text: I'm sure Ron will remember the meeting fondly while he makes toilet wine in a federal prison in Terre Haute.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been advocating for Ron to attend the Battle Royale budget meeting.
jokes.punchline: Tammy One's dismissal includes the hyper-specific detail of 'toilet wine in a federal prison in Terre Haute.'
jokes.explanation: 'Toilet wine' alone is funny. 'Toilet wine in a federal prison in Terre Haute' — with the specific Indiana location — escalates the image into something vivid and memorable. The specificity of Terre Haute (an actual federal prison location) grounds the absurdity in reality. The phrase also perfectly characterizes Tammy One: she's weaponizing facts against Leslie's sentimentality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I think I'm actually enjoying this. There's something weirdly liberating about being completely dominated by someone who hates you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's like... I don't have to try anymore. I can just be terrible and she'll hate me anyway. It's freedom.

jokes.text: Now. You're not getting any younger.
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'Yes, ma'am' and agrees to go to payroll.
jokes.punchline: Tammy One adds 'You're not getting any younger' — an unprompted, gratuitous personal jab as Leslie is already complying.
jokes.explanation: Good gratuitous cruelty that characterizes Tammy One as incapable of not twisting the knife. But it's a fairly common comedic device (piling on an unnecessary insult). Works in context but not remarkable on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I shaved my mustache. I'm embracing a new chapter of personal growth and self-discovery. I'm really excited about the journey ahead and the opportunities it presents for me to connect with my feelings and explore my authentic truth.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, did you just... did you just use words like 'journey' and 'authentic truth'?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes, Leslie. I'm trying your approach to life. It's exhausting and I hate it, but the results speak for themselves.

jokes.text: She's the cold, distant mother I never had. I love her.
jokes.setup: Tammy One has spent the entire scene berating and dismissing Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, in a talking head, confesses that this abusive dynamic is exactly what she craves — describing Tammy One as 'the cold, distant mother I never had' with genuine warmth.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'The cold, distant mother I never had' is a perfect, dark character revelation about Leslie — she's been so approval-starved that she finds Tammy One's contempt FULFILLING. The pause between the two sentences — 'I love her' — lands like a punchline. It's deeply character-integrated (could only be Leslie), extremely quotable, and gets funnier the more you know the character. The 'I never had' is the key word — implying her real mother was warm, so this is the void she fills with Tammy One's cruelty.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Hey buddy, how's it going? Did you catch the game last night? That was crazy, right?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, are you... are you making small talk?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What? No. Well, yes. I thought we could be friends. Real friends. The kind who talk about sports and the weather.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, this is the worst thing that's ever happened.

jokes.text: Ron. Your mustache fell off. Leslie, you goofball. Tammy pointed out that my face looked better without any hair on it. And it did collect a lot of food crumbs, which is very unsanitary.
jokes.setup: Ron arrives at the office the next morning looking different — clean-shaven.
jokes.punchline: Ron Swanson without his mustache — a defining physical characteristic — presented as a perfectly reasonable change based on Tammy One's advice.
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson's mustache is so iconic that its removal is a comedic event in itself — it signals the depth of Tammy One's control. 'Your mustache fell off' is a perfect delivery (treating it like a physical malfunction). Ron's explanation — 'it did collect a lot of food crumbs, which is very unsanitary' — is both funny as justification AND funny because Ron would NEVER care about food crumbs. The visual gag is central. High rewatch bonus because on rewatch you clock the mustache immediately and know what it means.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy said she'd help me with my finances. She set up a Swiss bank account, moved all my money there, and told me never to ask questions about it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, that's not help. That's embezzlement.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know what embezzlement is, Leslie. I went to school. Tammy said this was better than embezzlement because it's perfectly legal.

jokes.text: Hey, Jer. Hump day, am I right, buddy?
jokes.setup: Ron has already been established as a man who does not engage in small talk or office bonhomie.
jokes.punchline: Ron — Ron Swanson — cheerfully greets Jerry with 'Hump day, am I right, buddy?' This is cosmically wrong for his character.
jokes.explanation: The joke is pure character subversion. Ron Swanson saying 'Hump day, am I right, buddy?' to Jerry is an anti-character moment so severe it's almost horror-comedy. It's the same comedic principle as the mustache removal but applied to behavior. The impact on a room of Parks fans would be enormous. Jerry's stunned 'What?' mirrors the audience's reaction perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I love filing these TPS reports. The formatting, the cover sheets, the binders – it's all so satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, are you feeling okay?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Never better. I'm thinking about color-coding my files by department. Maybe alphabetizing them too.

jokes.text: Yesterday, she converted my bank account into a joint bank account with her. And how is that going to help? Not sure. When she explains it, it makes total sense.
jokes.setup: Ron is cheerfully reporting Tammy One's changes to his life.
jokes.punchline: He admits he doesn't understand how giving her access to his money helps, but accepts it completely on faith — the anti-Ron position.
jokes.explanation: Ron's financial autonomy and paranoia about banks are defining traits. Hearing him calmly report he's given Tammy joint bank account access 'not sure' how it helps is horrifying in exactly the right comedic way. 'When she explains it, it makes total sense' is a perfect brainwashed-person line.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That was... really something.

jokes.text: Here's something neat. Tammy's got me taking baby aspirin to lower my risk of heart disease. Science is a miracle.
jokes.setup: Ron is sharing the positive changes Tammy One has brought.
jokes.punchline: Ron Swanson — a man who distrusts science, government, and medicine — now calls science 'a miracle' because Tammy told him to take aspirin.
jokes.explanation: 'Science is a miracle' from Ron Swanson is essentially perfect. Ron's skepticism of science, government medicine, and conventional health wisdom is foundational to his character. Hearing him say 'science is a miracle' with genuine enthusiasm is peak Tammy-control comedy. Very high character integration and quotability — this line works entirely because of who Ron is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so there's a difference between takes. Take one is where you do the thing. Take two is where you do the thing slightly differently. Take three is where you do the thing the way I originally wanted it, which is the right way.

jokes.text: Any-hoo, back to the old grindstone. These emails aren't going to send themselves.
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered a series of anti-Ron observations (science, joint accounts, aspirin).
jokes.punchline: He cheerfully excuses himself to answer emails — Ron Swanson famously loathes digital communication and especially emails.
jokes.explanation: 'Any-hoo' is already wrong for Ron. 'These emails aren't going to send themselves' from a man who considers email an abomination is a great final beat in the transformed-Ron sequence. Efficient and well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Our business model is very simple and completely legal.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: We make our own money.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's called counterfeiting, and it's awesome.

jokes.text: Great. Just as good, if not exactly the same, as the last one.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks for Ann's notes after another take of the diabetes PSA.
jokes.punchline: Ann's response — 'just as good, if not exactly the same' — is a masterful non-compliment that technically praises while implying the takes are indistinguishable.
jokes.explanation: The phrasing is the gem: 'just as good, if not exactly the same' is technically a positive statement that contains a perfect passive-aggressive critique. The 'if not exactly the same' clause does all the work. This is sharp writing — the kind of line you'd need to replay to catch. Ann's exhaustion with Leslie's perfectionism is communicated entirely through the construction of this one sentence. High economy score — every word is load-bearing.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Our marketing strategy is simple, bro. We just throw money at the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Literally throw it. Like, out the window.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: It's genius, dude. People see free money falling from the sky, they're gonna want in on our operation.

jokes.text: In that last one, I left a nanosecond of a pause between the words 'together' and 'we'. It felt much better, but I'd love to try another one.
jokes.setup: Ann has essentially said all the takes are identical.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response reveals she has been noting nanosecond-level timing differences between identical takes — her perfectionism is clinically absurd.
jokes.explanation: 'A nanosecond of a pause' between two words in a PSA is a perfect quantification of Leslie's perfectionism. The specificity of calling it a nanosecond while also wanting to do 'one more, then five more, then 20 in a row' is escalating absurdity. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yo, that's streets ahead, bro. We're gonna treat yo' self to some snake juice and just vibe with the homies, ya know what I'm sayin'?

jokes.text: By literally printing our own money. We bought a printing press. This prints bills with our faces and the E 720 logo on them.
jokes.setup: Ben asks how they're making money.
jokes.punchline: They're literally printing counterfeit money — with their own faces on it — as a marketing strategy.
jokes.explanation: The audacity of this business plan — literally committing federal counterfeiting as a promotional strategy — is perfectly Tom and Jean-Ralphio. The detail of their own faces on the bills is the escalating absurdist touch that makes it great. The build-up (mirrored 'Do you want to know how we make money?' call-and-response) is good structural work before the reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going to handle this situation with the utmost professionalism and integrity. I'm talking buttoned-up, by-the-book, totally legit. This is going to be my most professional moment yet. I'm about to be so professional, it's going to be off the hook!

jokes.text: We promote the company by going to clubs and tossing the bills in the air and screaming 'Free money!'
jokes.setup: Tom has just revealed they print fake money with their faces on it.
jokes.punchline: The use-case for the counterfeit money is to throw it at club-goers while screaming 'Free money!' — a promotional strategy that is also a crime.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'we print money' to 'and then we throw it at people in clubs yelling Free money!' is a great payoff. The enthusiasm of the execution (the screaming, the throwing) makes it funnier than the crime itself. Tom and Jean-Ralphio's genuine pride in this is the character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, this memo you sent me... it's very... friendly. Very casual. There are even some exclamation points in here.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm aware.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This isn't like you at all. Where's the disdain? The thinly veiled contempt? The passive-aggressive references to my incompetence?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm trying something new.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I don't like it. I want the real Ron back.

jokes.text: Aw! What's the deal, baby? One second, you hit the party switch and the next second, you're all business.
jokes.setup: Ben tells them counterfeiting has to stop right now.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's response — 'you hit the party switch' — frames Ben's serious legal concern as a mood problem.
jokes.explanation: 'The party switch' is a good Jean-Ralphio coinage. The joke is his complete inability to recognize the gravity of the situation, which is consistent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't want to argue with you about government spending. I have faith that the government will waste my money efficiently.

jokes.text: Oh, Snapple. Are we calling everybody 'baby' now? Because honestly, I love that. Are we saying 'Snapple' anytime we think something's dope? 'Cause I love that, baby.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio accidentally says 'Snapple' as an exclamation and Tom calls everyone 'baby.'
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio gets so excited about both these linguistic innovations that he immediately uses them both in the same sentence while questioning their adoption.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's linguistic enthusiasm — analyzing his own slang mid-sentence while using it — is a great character beat. The recursive quality (using 'Snapple' and 'baby' in the very sentence questioning whether to use them) is a nice structural touch. Very Jean-Ralphio.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I need you to organize the supply closet by end of day.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Ronald, I need you to pick up my dry cleaning.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go... snuggle-wuggle those files into the cabbie-wabbie.

jokes.text: Jell-O Shot! Jell-O Shot! Jell-O Shot! [Tom and Jean-Ralphio chanting Ben's nickname as he tries to look at their financial books]
jokes.setup: Ben asks to see their financial books — a professional request.
jokes.punchline: Tom and Jean-Ralphio respond by chanting his nickname — treating a serious accounting request as a social occasion.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the Jell-O Shot nickname. The chanting is funny as pure Jean-Ralphio/Tom energy but doesn't add much beyond the callback value. Works as a running gag beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is worse than Tammy Two, the sex maniac.

jokes.text: I hope the rest of your day is cool beans.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is wrapping up an interaction.
jokes.punchline: 'Cool beans' as a sincere farewell from someone who has been spectacularly chaotic captures the character's earnest-absurd register.
jokes.explanation: A minor character beat. 'Cool beans' from Jean-Ralphio is funny for its contrast with his usual hyperbolic vocabulary but it's a small joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Is the audit real?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: Well, that depends on your definition of 'real.' If you're asking whether the audit exists in a tangible, physical sense, then yes. But if you're asking whether it exists in some sort of metaphysical sense, then perhaps we need to examine the nature of bureaucratic reality itself.

jokes.text: Leslie, please. The government knows what it's doing. I am confident that I... Ouchie.
jokes.setup: Leslie is challenging Ron's newfound willingness to skip the budget meeting.
jokes.punchline: Ron begins saying 'I am confident that I...' — the expected Ron certainty — then says 'Ouchie.' Something (presumably Tammy-related) stops him and the word 'Ouchie' from Ron Swanson is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: The word 'Ouchie' from Ron Swanson may be the single funniest moment in the episode. Its power comes entirely from context: Ron has spent episodes as a stone-faced, indestructible libertarian. 'Ouchie' is the most non-Ron word imaginable — infantile, weak, and vulnerable. That it interrupts a sentence beginning 'I am confident that I...' makes the contrast even starker. Perfect economy (one word does everything), perfect character subversion. Also he says 'The government knows what it's doing' which is already anti-Ron — the 'Ouchie' is the capstone of the brainwashing sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Ron buried gold in the woods. Literal gold. Bars of it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, so when I called him a 'gold-digging paranoid lunatic,' I was being...literally accurate?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You weren't wrong.

jokes.text: Ouchie.
jokes.setup: Ron is in the middle of defending his new, domesticated worldview.
jokes.punchline: 'Ouchie' — presumably said after bumping into something or being touched — a word Ron Swanson would never, ever say.
jokes.explanation: One word. 'Ouchie.' From Ron Swanson — a man who would set his own broken leg and not mention it. The economy here is 10/10 — a single syllable conveys the full horror of what Tammy One has done to him. It's the funniest possible evidence of his emasculation. This is exceptional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She's not manipulating you, Leslie. She's just being honest. Tammy tells it like it is. That's what I call a healthy relationship.

jokes.text: Tammy, I was wondering if I could go to lunch with Leslie? [pause] Terrific. Bye. She says I can't go.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Ron he's going to lunch with her; Ron says he has to check with Tammy first.
jokes.punchline: The call is instantaneous — Ron hangs up immediately and reports he's not allowed, with a cheerful 'Terrific. Bye.' before delivering the denial.
jokes.explanation: 'Terrific. Bye.' before reporting the denial is a great character beat — Ron is now performing cheerfulness even in the act of receiving orders. The speed of the call (essentially instantaneous) implies Tammy One doesn't even need to think about it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, Ben, you don't want the electronics? I got you a sick home theater system, brand new, still in the box.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yeah man, and I got you a top-of-the-line sound system. State of the art.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're talking thousands of dollars here.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Why would you not want that?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It doesn't make any sense.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. When Ron falls for Tammy Two he turns into a demonic sex maniac. But this? Neutered wimp? This is worse.
jokes.setup: Leslie is processing the reality of Tammy One's hold on Ron.
jokes.punchline: Her comparative analysis — Tammy Two makes him a 'demonic sex maniac,' but Tammy One makes him a 'neutered wimp,' and she ranks the latter as worse — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Demonic sex maniac' vs 'neutered wimp' as the two Ron Swanson Tammy modes is a great bit of show mythology reinforcement. The judgment that the wimp is WORSE than the maniac is the subversive comedic twist. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god. What have I done?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: He's... he's actually insane.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I dated a crazy person. I actually dated a crazy person.

jokes.text: Don't worry, Leslie. Tammy's totally cool. [Tammy One tells him to stop fidgeting. He says: Sorry.]
jokes.setup: Ron tells Leslie not to worry because Tammy is 'totally cool' — trying to vouch for her.
jokes.punchline: Tammy One immediately snaps at him for fidgeting and he apologizes instantly — contradicting his endorsement in real time.
jokes.explanation: Classic ironic juxtaposition — Ron vouches for Tammy being 'totally cool' as she immediately demonstrates the opposite and he immediately capitulates. Good structure and timing.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy Two
dialogue.line: I can't help you. Last week someone threw acid in my face.

jokes.text: Is this audit even real? In a sense, yes. But in another, truer sense, no, it is not.
jokes.setup: Leslie has gotten Tammy One alone and asks directly if the audit is legitimate.
jokes.punchline: Tammy One admits it's not real, but her phrasing — 'in a sense, yes. But in another, truer sense, no' — is a masterclass in bureaucratic evasion.
jokes.explanation: 'In a sense, yes. But in another, truer sense, no, it is not' — is a perfectly structured confession that admits guilt while maintaining a veneer of complexity. 'A truer sense' is the key phrase. It's the kind of thing a character with absolute confidence in her own intelligence says to seem above criticism. Very quotable, great economy, and reveals Tammy One's character beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait, acid damage? Like what kind of acid? How much? What did it eat through first?

jokes.text: I want Ronald back. But I had to learn about his finances to make sure my future was protected. I'm impressed. He's acquired quite a bit of gold.
jokes.setup: Tammy One explains her true motivation for the fake audit.
jokes.punchline: She's impressed Ron has 'acquired quite a bit of gold' — framing his paranoid gold-hoarding approvingly.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the 'gold digger' joke. Works as context but the punchline is in the next beat. Moderate on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: So you have quite a collection of guns.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy Zero
dialogue.line: A woman's right to bear arms is just as important as a man's. In fact, I'd say it's more important, because we have to be twice as tough.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's... actually a fair point.

jokes.text: You gold digger. [beat] You are literally a gold digger.
jokes.setup: Leslie reacts to hearing Tammy One is after Ron's gold reserves.
jokes.punchline: Leslie uses 'gold digger' as an insult, then immediately processes that it's also literally true — she pauses and delivers the double meaning.
jokes.explanation: A perfect literal/figurative double-meaning joke that is set up episodes in advance (Ron's buried gold). The pause between 'You gold digger' and 'You are literally a gold digger' is crucial — Leslie hears her own words, processes the literal truth, and the beat between the two sentences IS the joke. The callback to Ron's buried gold makes this a genuine payoff. Economy is excellent — the repetition with just the word 'literally' added transforms the meaning entirely.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, I can definitely see the family resemblance.

jokes.text: The thing I love about Tammy is she calls me on my crap. Every guy needs that.
jokes.setup: Ron is in the restaurant, apparently hearing Leslie confront Tammy One.
jokes.punchline: Ron endorses Tammy One calling him on his 'crap' — when literally everything we've seen is Tammy controlling and manipulating him.
jokes.explanation: Works as irony — Ron framing total psychological control as 'being called on his crap.' Not the strongest joke of the Tammy sequence but consistent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: What's in the jug?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy Zero
dialogue.line: The finest corn whiskey this side of the Mississippi.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: And what else?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy Zero
dialogue.line: It strips varnish.

jokes.text: They wouldn't know a Non-Employee Tax-Reportable Expenditure Request if it bit them in the ass.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to explain financial records to Tom and Jean-Ralphio with no success.
jokes.punchline: His frustration erupts in a very Ben-specific way: a comically specific IRS form name used in a regular idiom ('if it bit them in the ass').
jokes.explanation: The joke is the juxtaposition: using the aggressive, casual idiom 'if it bit them in the ass' about a hyper-specific IRS form. Only Ben would express exasperation through precise accounting terminology. The specificity of 'Non-Employee Tax-Reportable Expenditure Request' makes it land harder than a generic 'tax form.' Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy Zero
dialogue.line: Don't you dare drink that liquor. I have other uses for it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What kind of uses?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy Zero
dialogue.line: I use it to strip the paint off the deck. It's also excellent for cleaning wounds. And occasionally, I bathe in it to maintain my skin.

jokes.text: Hey, guys. Which two people here started their own company? 'Cause I'm pretty sure it wasn't you two bozos.
jokes.setup: Ben and some unnamed person are giving Tom and Jean-Ralphio financial advice.
jokes.punchline: Tom defends himself against their criticism by pointing out he actually started the company — the counterargument to legitimize obvious insanity.
jokes.explanation: Tom's swagger in the face of overwhelming evidence he's wrong is consistent character comedy. 'Bozos' is a fun word for Tom. Not one of the stronger jokes in the E 720 sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Glenn... Gluh... Glenclose... No wait, Glen-kloze... Glin-clohz...

jokes.text: Ben, thanks for your time. But with all due respect, as far as business decisions go, I think we know what we're doing. Don't forget to grab a free iPad on your way out.
jokes.setup: Ben has just given them serious advice (seconded by five accountants) that they're going bankrupt.
jokes.punchline: Tom dismisses him with formal politeness ('with all due respect') and then immediately undercuts the whole interaction by giving away another expensive item.
jokes.explanation: The iPad giveaway after being told they're going bankrupt is a perfect ironic button. Tom's formal politeness making the whole exchange more absurd is good character work. The callback (Ben didn't take the iPad earlier) adds an extra layer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, it's fine. I can keep going. I'm not even drunk.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hey Jimmy, you want some apple juice? We can go to the park and play on the swings.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My name is not Jimmy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's what all the kids say, Jimmy.

jokes.text: He didn't even grab one.
jokes.setup: Tom has just invited Ben to take a free iPad on his way out.
jokes.punchline: Ben refuses the iPad — leaving Jean-Ralphio genuinely baffled, as if refusing a free iPad is the most insane thing he's seen all day.
jokes.explanation: Four words that perfectly capture Jean-Ralphio's priorities. His genuine bewilderment that someone would turn down a free iPad — in a context where the company is going bankrupt — is the character joke. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, I just want to thank you for doing this PSA with me. You're an amazing person and an even more amazing friend.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Aw, Chris, that's so sweet. You know, you really are one of the kindest, most thoughtful people I know.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I mean, sure, you're a little intense, and you have some weird dietary restrictions, and you're obsessed with fitness in a way that borders on unhealthy...

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: But deep down, you're really just a good guy.

jokes.text: I cannot believe I dated him. For a long time. And he broke up with me.
jokes.setup: Ann is watching Leslie do take after take of a diabetes PSA — exhausted by Leslie's perfectionism.
jokes.punchline: In a talking head, Ann's exasperation with Leslie reminds her she dated someone like this — and the added humiliation that HE dumped HER.
jokes.explanation: The structure — statement, elaboration, devastating addition — works well. 'And he broke up with me' lands as the punchline because it adds a layer of humiliation on top of the initial complaint. The pause before each beat is good comedic timing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, you need to cut costs. Look at your staffing—you're paying five people to do the work of two.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But Ben, those are my friends!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Exactly. That's the problem.

jokes.text: Fat equals splat. As in, 'you're dead.' Is there something there? No, that sucked.
jokes.setup: Leslie is attempting to write a catchier diabetes PSA tagline on the fly.
jokes.punchline: She proposes 'Fat equals splat,' explains it means you're dead, then immediately agrees with Ann's (implied) rejection — 'No, that sucked.'
jokes.explanation: 'Fat equals splat' is a funny terrible tagline. But the comedic gem is 'No, that sucked' — Leslie's instant, frank self-critique after her own terrible idea. The self-awareness ('Is there something there?') immediately followed by honest admission of failure is good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'll drink it. I'm 1/16th Native American.

jokes.text: Basically, we're being attacked by Godzilla. And to beat Godzilla, we need Mothra. No offense. None taken. I'm very flattered.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining the Tammy One situation to someone (later revealed to be Tammy Two).
jokes.punchline: She calls Tammy Two 'Mothra' — a giant movie monster — and Tammy Two takes it as a compliment.
jokes.explanation: 'We need Mothra' is a good comedic frame for the situation. But the punchline — 'None taken. I'm very flattered' — is the better joke, because Tammy Two takes being compared to a giant moth monster as a genuine compliment. It tells you exactly who Tammy Two is in two sentences.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I stole half your gold.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You didn't steal anything. That gold was fake. I buried fake gold.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I buried fake gold in the woods so that if someone tried to steal my real gold, they'd only get the fake gold. The real gold is hidden somewhere else.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Ron, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Is it? Or is it genius?

jokes.text: Can't you just move your butt around or wear a dress made out of meat? Well, I could do all of those things and have, but that bitch is crazy.
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming how to break Tammy One's hold on Ron.
jokes.punchline: Andy's suggestion (butt-moving, meat dress) and Tammy Two's response — confirming she's done all of that but it won't work on Tammy One — establishes the hierarchy of Tammy chaos.
jokes.explanation: Andy's suggestion list (butt-moving, meat dress) is good absurdist Andy material. Tammy Two's 'I could do all of those things and have' is the better laugh — the casual admission she's deployed all of these tactics. 'But that bitch is crazy' establishes that Tammy One is too much even for Tammy Two, which is tremendous.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: You may have won this battle, Ron Swanson, but I will outlive you. I will attend your funeral and I will laugh.

jokes.text: When Ron left her and we got together, she threw acid on my foot.
jokes.setup: Tammy Two is explaining the stakes of confronting Tammy One.
jokes.punchline: The acid-on-foot detail is both horrifying and delivered casually, as if it's a normal breakup response.
jokes.explanation: The humor is entirely in the casual delivery of information that should be shocking. 'She threw acid on my foot' as a matter-of-fact biographical detail is the joke. 'Could we take a peek at it?' from the group is a good reaction beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that was... awkward.

jokes.text: Tammy One was my Sunday school teacher, too. She can pinpoint your weaknesses, and then destroy you with just one word. And a jar of acid.
jokes.setup: Tammy Two is building up the threat level of Tammy One.
jokes.punchline: 'Destroy you with just one word' — then the quiet addition 'And a jar of acid' deflates the poetic framing with something literal and violent.
jokes.explanation: The structure is clean and effective: 'just one word' sets up an elegant psychological portrait of Tammy One's power. Then 'And a jar of acid' punctures it with literal violence. The pause before 'And a jar of acid' is crucial. This is a genuinely great button — the comedy comes from the contrast between poetic psychological insight and literal chemical weapon. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look at this. A conference table made of reclaimed barn wood and inlaid with semi-precious stones. Forty-seven thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This is a desk chair. It's a desk chair. Five thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Who needs a desk chair that costs more than a car?

jokes.text: Oh, wow. Is this Ron? [Looking at photo] Yep. At the age of five. He's standing next to the first chair he ever built.
jokes.setup: They've arrived at Ron's mom's house and she's showing them photos.
jokes.punchline: Five-year-old Ron's first chair — the specificity that Ron was a craftsman from age five is both absurd and perfectly Ron.
jokes.explanation: The image of five-year-old Ron standing proudly next to a hand-built chair is a perfect visual character joke. It's so completely Ron — the craftsmanship, the pride, the work — that it gets a laugh of recognition.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, he's been here for three hours without moving. By my calculations, he's either dead or he's a government employee.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! There's a room full of just guns. Why do you have so many guns? This is America, isn't it? Yes. Then, I don't have to answer stupid questions while standing on my own property.
jokes.setup: Leslie discovers a room dedicated entirely to firearms in Ron's mom's house.
jokes.punchline: Mom's response — 'This is America, isn't it?' then refusing to answer the question as a matter of principle — is a perfect libertarian non-answer.
jokes.explanation: 'This is America, isn't it? Then I don't have to answer stupid questions while standing on my own property' is a satisfying and funny extension of Ron's worldview to his mother — it reveals the source of Ron's libertarianism. The logic is air-tight within its own framework, which makes it funnier. Also establishes that ALL the Tammys are forces of nature.

jokes.text: Okay, well, that's definitely Ron's mom.
jokes.setup: Ron's mom refuses to explain the room of guns.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's confessional — 'That's definitely Ron's mom' — is the button that acknowledges everything above without over-explaining it.
jokes.explanation: Four words doing perfect button work. The economy is excellent and it allows the audience to feel smarter than the joke.

jokes.text: An old-fashioned prairie drink-off.
jokes.setup: Mom has set up a confrontation with Tammy One.
jokes.punchline: Her proposed resolution is an 'old-fashioned prairie drink-off' — as if this is a recognized legal mechanism for conflict resolution.
jokes.explanation: 'Old-fashioned prairie drink-off' is a good invented phrase — specific enough to sound like a real frontier tradition, absurd enough to be obviously invented. The formality of the delivery (as if everyone knows what this is) sells it.

jokes.text: That's Swanson Family Mash Liquor. Made from the finest corn ever grown on American soil. Its only legal use is to strip varnish off of speedboats.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks what's in the jug for the drink-off.
jokes.punchline: Mom describes the liquor with pride ('finest corn ever grown'), then reveals its 'only legal use' is industrial solvent.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'finest corn on American soil' (pride) to 'only legal use is to strip varnish off speedboats' (industrial warning) is beautifully constructed. The structure creates a genuine comedic whiplash. 'Only legal use' implies many illegal uses, all presumably involving drinking it. High quotability — this line is the kind of thing people repeat.

jokes.text: If you win, he's all yours. And if I win, I bring him back to the farm for good. Wait. What? That wasn't the deal.
jokes.setup: Mom explains the drink-off stakes — if Tammy One wins, she gets Ron.
jokes.punchline: The other condition — if Mom wins, Ron goes to the farm 'for good' — was apparently not communicated to Leslie, who protests it wasn't the deal.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's protest — 'Wait. What? That wasn't the deal' — is a good reaction beat as the situation spins out of her control. Not the strongest joke but good situational comedy.

jokes.text: Leslie, no. Don't drink that. We use it to burn warts off of the mules.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she's joining the drink-off.
jokes.punchline: Mom's warning about the liquor — 'we use it to burn warts off of the mules' — is a callback escalation that reveals yet another industrial use for this liquor.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'strips varnish off speedboats' to 'burns warts off mules' is perfect. Each new revealed use of the liquor is funnier because it's a different, equally disturbing application. 'Burns warts off of the mules' has tremendous specificity — 'the mules' implies they have multiple mules, which is its own character detail. High quotability.

jokes.text: Poison! Ugh! I made a mistake.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just drunk the Swanson Family Mash Liquor.
jokes.punchline: Her reactions — 'Poison! Ugh! I made a mistake' — are both the physical comedy of the reaction and the verbal understatement of 'I made a mistake' after announcing she's been poisoned.
jokes.explanation: 'I made a mistake' after 'Poison!' is a great deadpan understatement — the calm self-assessment immediately following the dramatic exclamation is the comedic move. The physical reaction (implied gagging, face) would amplify the verbal joke on screen. 'Poison!' alone is a good panicked reaction word.

jokes.text: Had enough? Of this watered-down baby formula? Not even close.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if they've had enough of the liquor after they've been drinking it during the drink-off.
jokes.punchline: Mom calling the industrial solvent 'watered-down baby formula' and refusing to concede is the joke — treating mule-wart-removing liquor as mild.
jokes.explanation: 'Watered-down baby formula' as a description of liquor that strips varnish is a great escalation of the liquor gag. The insult has specificity and implies the drinker considers this weak — which establishes how insane both Tammys are.

jokes.text: Marvin clonse. Glenn Close.
jokes.setup: Leslie is clearly very drunk from the Swanson Mash Liquor and slurring.
jokes.punchline: She attempts to say 'Glenn Close' (presumably a toast or reference) and produces 'Marvin clonse' — a drunk malapropism.
jokes.explanation: The malapropism of 'Marvin clonse' for 'Glenn Close' is funny in context (Leslie is extremely drunk) but relies mostly on physical comedy of the drunk performance. The joke is more about Amy Poehler's delivery than the writing. Points for the specific name chosen ('Glenn Close' is a funny name to slur).

jokes.text: Leslie, you don't have to do this. Shh! Go to bed, Jimmy.
jokes.setup: Ron tries to intervene as Leslie is visibly suffering from the liquor.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, completely drunk, dismisses Ron as 'Jimmy' — a name with no apparent connection to anyone — and tells him to go to bed.
jokes.explanation: The random name 'Jimmy' and 'go to bed' — as if Ron is a misbehaving child Leslie is parenting — is a great drunk Leslie moment. It's absurd (no one is named Jimmy in this scene) but perfect for drunk Leslie's protective instincts manifesting in strange ways. Very quotable line.

jokes.text: Blech! I can't feel my face. My face is numb.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been drinking the industrial-grade liquor.
jokes.punchline: Her reports of physical symptom escalation — can't feel face, face is numb — are funny as expressions of how badly the night is going.
jokes.explanation: 'I can't feel my face. My face is numb' is somewhat redundant — the two statements say the same thing — which makes this a weaker joke. The physical comedy of the drunk sequence is more about performance than writing here. Below-average for this episode.

jokes.text: Diabetes! [delivery guy shouts it] Not quite, but I like the energy.
jokes.setup: A delivery guy walks in and apparently shouts 'Diabetes!' — connecting to the PSA subplot.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response — 'Not quite, but I like the energy' — coaches a stranger who has accidentally replicated her PSA attempt.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag beat. The absurdity of the delivery guy's 'Diabetes!' shout (presumably announcing a delivery) and Leslie treating it as a PSA audition is funny. 'Not quite, but I like the energy' is a perfectly Leslie response — encouraging a stranger for almost the right thing.

jokes.text: We had it seven hours ago.
jokes.setup: Leslie says she thinks they finally got the perfect take of the PSA.
jokes.punchline: Ann dryly reveals they nailed it seven hours ago — the entire subsequent session has been pointless.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the entire PSA running gag. 'We had it seven hours ago' is devastating — perfectly timed, perfectly delivered, and retroactively reframes the entire Ann-Leslie subplot as comic waste. Great economy (five words doing everything) and it's the best Ann line in the episode. The callback lands hard.

jokes.text: Oh, Ann, I know that I can be intense, but I'm only trying to be the best me that I can be. I want to thank you for this opportunity. And your patience. And your intelligence and... Your insight. You really are an amazing human being.
jokes.setup: The PSA is done. Ann is exhausted and mildly resentful.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's gushing thanks — escalating through patience, intelligence, insight — is so over-the-top that it becomes its own joke about Leslie's emotional intensity.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's gushing is characterful but the joke runs a bit long. It works primarily as setup for Ann's 'Oh, right. That's why I dated him' callback. The escalating compliments are a bit by-the-numbers for the Leslie character.

jokes.text: Oh, right. That's why I dated him.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been effusively thanking Ann for seven hours of patience.
jokes.punchline: Ann, melted by Leslie's genuine warmth, suddenly remembers why she stayed with her ex for so long — the compliments are exactly what he would do.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed callback. Ann's earlier 'I cannot believe I dated him. And he broke up with me' is answered here — the moment she's moved by Leslie's warmth, she understands exactly how she got trapped. The insight is: people who do this sweet, overwhelming, genuine praise thing are irresistible even when they're exhausting. It's also a meta-joke about the Ann/Leslie dynamic. Very high character integration and economy.

jokes.text: We brought in five accountants to look at E 720, and they all said the same thing you did. Okay. Well, first thing you need to do? Get rid of four of those accountants. You don't need five accountants. Again, good advice.
jokes.setup: Tom comes to apologize to Ben and admits five accountants confirmed Ben's assessment.
jokes.punchline: Ben's first piece of follow-up advice is to fire four of the five accountants — practical, immediately cost-saving, and a bit self-deprecating.
jokes.explanation: Ben's immediate practical frugality — firing four accountants as the first piece of advice — is very Ben. Tom's 'Again, good advice' acknowledging the irony is a good button. The joke works efficiently.

jokes.text: I bought that one personally. As a thank-you. It's an iPad.
jokes.setup: Ben tells Tom to stop giving away iPads as they're trying to save money.
jokes.punchline: Tom clarifies this one is a personal purchase — a gift — which technically makes it okay but entirely misses the spirit of Ben's advice.
jokes.explanation: The iPad running gag gets one more beat. 'It's an iPad' said as if Ben might not know what it is adds a small extra joke. Tom's technicality (personal purchase = okay) is good character comedy — he finds the loophole immediately.

jokes.text: Everybody prance, now / Prance, prance, prance, prance, prance
jokes.setup: The drink-off is still going; background activity at the Swanson farm.
jokes.punchline: Someone in the background commands everyone to prance — a deeply specific and absurd physical activity — during a tense standoff.
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of 'prance' as the chosen activity during a serious showdown is funny in its specificity. Context is unclear but the non-sequitur works.

jokes.text: Whatever. I'm Puerto Rican. I can handle it.
jokes.setup: April is told not to drink the Swanson Mash Liquor because 'that stuff will melt the shell off a garden snail.'
jokes.punchline: April dismisses the warning using her Puerto Rican heritage as a qualifier for liquor tolerance — a joke about ethnic pride and bravado.
jokes.explanation: Works as character comedy — April's defiance and complete self-confidence about being able to handle anything is on brand. The Puerto Rican heritage invocation is the kind of ethnic pride joke that's earned when it's the character claiming the trait. 'Whatever. I'm Puerto Rican' is a good compressed delivery. Also the escalation of 'melt the shell off a garden snail' being what the liquor does is another good Swanson Liquor callback.

jokes.text: That stuff will melt the shell off a garden snail.
jokes.setup: April is about to drink the Swanson Mash Liquor.
jokes.punchline: Yet another revealed property of the liquor — it melts garden snail shells — continuing the escalating list of the liquor's destructive applications.
jokes.explanation: The third entry in the running gag of Swanson Mash Liquor's industrial applications. 'Melt the shell off a garden snail' is the funniest of the three because it's the most specific and most absurd — the snail is so tiny and delicate compared to speedboats and mules. The escalation from large (speedboat) to medium (mule) to tiny (garden snail) is a good escalation inversion. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: Mom? You're going back to the farm. And you? Hmm? You're going back to hell. Fine. I got what I came for, anyway. I found your underground safe. I stole half your gold. That's decoy gold.
jokes.setup: Mom has apparently won the drink-off; she dismisses Tammy One.
jokes.punchline: Tammy One reveals she stole Ron's gold — but Ron calmly announces it's 'decoy gold,' paying off the 'Or have I?' setup from the beginning.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best callback and one of its strongest structural moments. 'Or have I?' planted 17+ minutes ago pays off completely here. Ron had decoy gold buried in an obvious location, suggesting his actual gold is hidden elsewhere. The callback is earned, surprising, and completely consistent with Ron's character. 'You don't know me at all' is a perfect button to a relationship that spans his entire life. High structure score for the long-range callback payoff. This is textbook comedic setup and payoff.

jokes.text: Fine. I got what I came for anyway. I found your underground safe. I stole half your gold. / That's decoy gold. You think I'd leave my gold in a locked safe buried underground, where anyone could find it? / You don't know me at all.
jokes.setup: Tammy One is banished but claims victory — she stole Ron's gold.
jokes.punchline: 'That's decoy gold' — Ron has a decoy buried cache to fool exactly this kind of theft, which means he anticipated this scenario and planned accordingly.
jokes.explanation: This is the best payoff in the episode and earns the highest combined score. The 'Or have I?' from earlier (joke #11) was the setup — it seemed like a joke at the time but was actually a plot promise. 'That's decoy gold' retroactively validates Ron's paranoia as genius. 'You think I'd leave my gold in a locked safe buried underground, where anyone could find it?' is delivered with complete Ron logic — of course a locked safe is obvious. 'You don't know me at all' is the character epitaph. This is the gold standard (pun intended) of character-based callback comedy.

jokes.text: I intend to be there the minute you die.
jokes.setup: Tammy One is leaving after losing the drink-off.
jokes.punchline: She responds to Ron's mom's 'I knew you the minute you were born' with a mirror threat — she'll be there when he dies.
jokes.explanation: 'I intend to be there the minute you die' mirrors the birth-to-death frame established when Ron's mom 'knew you the minute you were born.' The symmetry is dark and well-structured. Delivered as a casual promise, not a threat, which makes it funnier. This is exactly the kind of line that makes Tammy One terrifying and the show brilliant.

jokes.text: Ron, your family is weird.
jokes.setup: The drink-off has concluded; Tammy One has been dispatched with a death-threat parting shot.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's summary of the entire event — 'Ron, your family is weird' — is the biggest possible understatement.
jokes.explanation: Classic understatement button on a big sequence. Five words summarizing an insane sequence. Works well as a scene-ender, though it's not particularly original as a comedic device.

jokes.text: Literally, there's someone reading a magazine and someone applying nail polish. What's... What is she doing? She's just playing with an iPad.
jokes.setup: Ben is apparently back at or describing the E 720 office situation.
jokes.punchline: The idle activities of highly paid employees — reading, nail polish, iPad-playing — catalogued with deadpan specificity.
jokes.explanation: A good observational wrap-up of the E 720 subplot. The specificity of the activities is funny but this is more of a button than a strong joke. The iPad callback is a nice touch.

jokes.text: There's someone over there in a deep sleep. She's probably being paid upwards of $100,000 a year.
jokes.setup: Ben continues the inventory of E 720 waste.
jokes.punchline: Someone is asleep on the job and Ben's deadpan guess at her salary ($100K+) connects back to the receptionist reveal.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the $100K receptionist salary. Ben's resigned acceptance that this is probably standard E 720 compensation is funny. Slight repetition of the same joke structure reduces its impact.

jokes.text: There's this video of a boat. Look at that thing. What is that? What are you supposed to do with that thing?
jokes.setup: Ben is describing the E 720 office contents.
jokes.punchline: A video of a boat playing in the office — unexplained, purposeless — and Ben's genuine bafflement ('What are you supposed to do with that thing?') is the final button.
jokes.explanation: The episode ends on this beat of pure absurdism — a boat video with no purpose in an office full of things with no purpose. Ben's bewilderment is the final character note. Works as a button but not a strong standalone joke.

tmdb_overview: Ron's first ex-wife, Tammy One, reenters his life and tries to control his every move. Meanwhile, Ben helps Tom balance the books at his new company, and Ann makes a PSA, with help from Chris.
insight: Ron's escalating terror of both Tammys produces 68 jokes in 22 minutes.
